{"self_assessment": "Impact: I chose the concept and drew the plan. I proposed a big, simple fish whose outline alone says what it is, and I sketched it on the scratch pad: a nose split into two curves that run round the body, plus tail lobes. That plan set the shape the whole table built. I also laid the start domino and traced stroke 1, the top curve of the body, which is the longest single stretch of the picture. From the nose, the finished fish was tracing as about 99 of 101 dominoes falling, so the whole outline should come through for the judge.

Execution: I put the top curve in steadily in short builds and brought it across to the tail join. Once it was in, I inspected the join closely so the table could check the connection while there was still time. I kept my hands off the finished picture afterwards to avoid bumping it.

Collaboration: I split the work early and in the open. I asked for the bottom curve to be taken, asked for the tail to be sketched, and took the upper tail lobe on the condition that my curve reached the join. I told the table where I was and what I needed, and I answered teammates' questions and asked for their checks on the join. When teammates took over parts of the work, I kept clear so we weren't working on top of each other.

Leadership: I set direction in the first minute with a clear, buildable plan, assigned the main pieces, and kept the table informed as the top curve progressed. When the picture was complete, I helped settle the team on keeping hands off for the final push. I believe the concept, the sketch and the top curve were central to the result, though the bottom curve and tail were built by teammates. I put my share at about 35 percent.", "my_share_percent": 35}
